I’ll inspect the discussion, then trace the relevant code and tests in this repository. I’ll report the likely cause and concrete fix options without changing anything yet.

The report matches the current success path: the mutation check happens only after rustc has written its outputs, and its error is downgraded to a warning while the shim returns rustc’s successful status. I’m now checking exactly which outputs can be safely invalidated and how Cargo’s dep-info/fingerprint behavior affects the smallest reliable fix.

A key nuance is that this should not be handled as a generic “cache publication failed” cleanup. Store/network/serialization failures leave a valid local compiler result; only evidence that an input changed during the compile (including the post-hash race) warrants invalidating the local output set. I’m validating that distinction with a deterministic delayed-compiler reproduction.

content.text:
The report identifies a real correctness bug, though I could not reproduce one detail of the explanation.

I built a deterministic compiler proxy that paused after rustc produced metadata, edited the source and dependent, then let mbx continue. With Cargo 1.96 and managed targets:

- mbx detected `InputModifiedDuringCompilation`.
- It downgraded that to “result was not stored.”
- It returned rustc’s successful exit status.
- Cargo immediately compiled the dependent against the pre-edit `.rmeta`, producing the reported missing-function error.

The cause is clear in [rustc.rs](/Users/jdx/src/mr-boxington/crates/mbx/src/rustc.rs:455): input verification happens after rustc succeeds, but every publication error becomes a warning at [line 499](/Users/jdx/src/mr-boxington/crates/mbx/src/rustc.rs:499), and the successful compiler status is returned at line 508. The same behavior remains on current `origin/main`; #300 does not address it.

One caveat: I could not reproduce the next invocation considering the source crate `Fresh`. In both ordinary and managed targets, Cargo 1.96 marked it dirty because the edited source was newer than Cargo’s pre-compilation freshness anchor. That agrees with [Cargo’s fingerprint documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/nightly-rustc/cargo/core/compiler/fingerprint/index.html). A `CARGO_LOG=cargo::core::compiler::fingerprint=trace` log from the affected environment would help explain that persistent-freshness detail. It may require an additional timestamp, filesystem, or dependency-output condition.

Recommended fix:

- Treat `InputModifiedDuringCompilation` and `InputChanged` as compilation-integrity failures, not ordinary cache-publication failures.
- Remove every modeled artifact in `RustcOutputs.files` plus its dep-info.
- Return failure instead of rustc’s successful status, preventing Cargo from scheduling dependents or completing a successful fingerprint.
- Continue treating storage, network, and serialization failures as warnings; those do not invalidate the local compiler result.
- Add a deterministic delayed-compiler integration test covering the mutation and asserting that no stale dependent compilation can proceed.

No repository files were changed.
make a pr, post a reply

I’ll implement the integrity-failure path on a fresh branch from current `origin/main`, add a deterministic regression test, run the focused and broader checks, then push a review-ready PR and reply to discussion #325 with the findings and link.

The implementation will keep ordinary cache-publication failures non-fatal, but split out the two typed mutation errors. For those, mbx will delete the complete modeled output set and return failure, so Cargo cannot launch dependents or bless the unit as successfully compiled.

content.text: I found the Windows-specific root cause: `exit_code(output.status)` is intentionally non-returning on Windows because it calls `ExitProcess` to preserve the full status code. My refactor evaluated it before publication, so every successful rustc shim exited before storing or recording its result. I’m replacing that eager conversion with a mutation flag and preserving the original end-of-function conversion.

what on earth could we do?

The gap looks architectural, not like “make hashing 10% faster.” rust-cache restores Cargo’s whole target tree, so Cargo schedules almost nothing; mbx starts with an empty target tree, causing Cargo to launch roughly 720 wrapper invocations even though all become cache hits. I’m checking whether mbx already records enough output metadata to add a batch “hydrate target” path—the most plausible way to erase that scheduling/process overhead.

content.text: yeah but if we make a small edit... does that not make things better for us?

Yes—the test did make a small edit: 30 lines in one hk Rust source file, with the same `Cargo.lock`.

It helped mbx, but helped rust-cache more:

- rust-cache restores the complete Cargo target tree. Cargo sees every dependency as fresh and recompiles only the hk crate.
- mbx restores its object store into an empty target directory. Cargo still schedules roughly 720 compiler commands; mbx turns those into hits, but invoking and processing 720 hits costs time. It then also recompiles hk.

So this scenario is almost rust-cache’s ideal case. To win it, mbx needs to restore/hydrate the prior target tree before Cargo starts, so Cargo schedules only the edited crate. Per-compiler cache hits alone won’t beat a fully restored Cargo build graph.
keep exploring

I’m going to test the missing case directly: keep a fully hydrated mbx target from the parent build, switch to the one-file child commit, and measure the edit without forcing Cargo to rediscover 720 cached dependencies. That tells us the ceiling for a future “restore target snapshot” feature and whether wrapper overhead on the changed hk crate still prevents a win.

That delay is outside the benchmark timer, but it makes iteration painfully slow. After the active 1.7 measurement finishes, I’m switching this temporary runner to one persistent session for the remaining jobs.

content.text:
Yes—the warm-ish small-edit scenario can beat rust-cache, but only with Cargo scheduling-state hydration.

Across three paired GHA trials using fresh parent caches:

| | Median restore + build | Median build |
|---|---:|---:|
| rust-cache | 40.05s | 22.56s |
| hydrated mbx | 39.13s | 22.64s |

That is:

- 2.3% lower median wall time for mbx
- mbx won 2 of 3 trials
- 11.8% smaller transported cache: 408 MiB versus 463 MiB
- Very stable mbx totals: 38.68–39.13s
- No meaningful compilation advantage; the win is entirely restoration efficiency

Runs: [fresh caches](https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington/actions/runs/33825236055), [repeat 1](https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington/actions/runs/33826115865), [repeat 2](https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington/actions/runs/33826378784).

The shipping action still does not achieve this. It restores mbx’s compilation objects but loses Cargo’s scheduling state, causing ~40–47s edited builds instead of ~22.6s. The prototype preserves Cargo’s metadata tree as a sidecar and materializes CAS-backed outputs into it.

Version-wise, 1.6 and 1.7 are effectively flat: both produced ~408 MiB archives and ~22.6s edited builds. Earlier apparent swings were GitHub cache/network variance, not an mbx performance change. A credible historical graph therefore needs paired repetitions, medians/ranges, archive bytes, and separate restore/hydrate/build phases per released version.

The experimental branch is pushed at `codex/benchmark-small-edit`; no PR yet. The next substantive step is implementing this workspace-state sidecar in mbx/action proper, then promoting the benchmark and recording release history. The perf box has been restored to its normal dispatcher configuration.
how does it work?

The prototype combines mbx’s content-addressed cache with just enough of Cargo’s `target` directory to preserve Cargo’s incremental scheduling decisions.

```text
Parent build
  │
  ├─ mbx CAS: compiled dependency outputs
  ├─ Cargo metadata: fingerprints, dep-info, build-script state
  └─ Cargo registry
          │
          ▼
     GitHub cache
          │
          ▼
Small-edit build
  │
  ├─ restore metadata tree directly with tar
  ├─ materialize compiled outputs from mbx CAS
  ├─ regenerate mbx build-script shims
  └─ run cargo → only the edited hk crate rebuilds
```

During the parent build, the snapshotter examines every file in Cargo’s `target` directory:

- Files already represented in mbx’s CAS are recorded as references rather than duplicated.
- Cargo-only state—fingerprints, dependency metadata, and build-script state—is stored directly in a sparse metadata tree.
- mbx-generated shims are recorded symbolically and regenerated during restore.
- File modes, modification times, directories, and genuine hardlinks are preserved because Cargo uses this state to decide what is fresh.

On the child commit, GitHub’s cache action extracts the metadata tree and Cargo registry. The hydrator then reflinks the referenced outputs from the restored mbx CAS into their expected `target` paths. This takes about 2 seconds on the perf box. Cargo consequently sees a normal warm target directory and recompiles only `hk`.

The distinction is:

| Approach | What Cargo sees after restore |
|---|---|
| Current mbx action | Compilation objects exist in mbx, but Cargo’s target state is absent, so Cargo schedules substantial work again |
| rust-cache | Almost the entire Cargo target directory is restored |
| Hydrated mbx | Cargo state is restored, while large compiled outputs are deduplicated through mbx’s CAS |

That is why the hydrated archive is about 408 MiB versus rust-cache’s 463 MiB while producing the same ~22.6-second small-edit build.

For production, this should become a workspace-state sidecar in `mbx cache export/import`, with the action transporting it alongside the existing closure bundle. The Python code is a proof of that format and restore procedure, not something we would ship as the final implementation.
wait a tic, is this basically doubling the cache?

Logically, it creates two views of the build, but it does **not** store two full copies of the artifacts.

- The mbx CAS contains compiled artifact bytes once.
- The Cargo sidecar contains scheduler metadata, fingerprints, dep-info, directory metadata, and references to CAS objects.
- During restore, target artifacts are reflinked from the CAS, so they appear in both places without duplicating physical blocks.

The measured archive was ~408 MiB versus rust-cache’s ~463 MiB, so the prototype is actually about 12% smaller—not doubled.

The caveat: our prototype caches the raw mbx store plus every target file it cannot associate with a CAS object. That is broader than an ideal implementation and may duplicate some non-CAS artifacts. Before promoting this, we should report a byte breakdown of:

1. CAS objects
2. Cargo metadata sidecar
3. non-CAS target files
4. registry

If the non-CAS bucket is large, we’d need to tighten the design. The intended production form is “CAS closure + relatively small Cargo-state sidecar,” not “mbx cache + another complete `target/`.”

content.text:
Done. The measurement confirms we are not doubling the cache.

| Component | Uncompressed |
|---|---:|
| CAS objects | 1,349.45 MiB |
| Cargo registry | 287.50 MiB |
| mbx metadata | 20.20 MiB |
| Cargo inline state | 55.14 MiB |
| Cargo manifest | 0.65 MiB |

The added hydration sidecar is **55.78 MiB**, or only **3.37% overhead**. It references another 2,397.8 MiB of logical target files without storing those bytes again.

Actual GitHub archives:

- Hydrated mbx: **408.33 MiB**
- rust-cache: **462.93 MiB**
- mbx is **11.8% smaller**

The clean timing repeat was 37.97 s for hydrated mbx versus 36.47 s for rust-cache. Across all four valid trials, the medians are effectively tied: **38.90 s mbx versus 38.98 s rust-cache**.

Instrumentation is pushed in commits `8fab58a` and `a3810d8`. [Fresh composition run](https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington/actions/runs/33827619024) · [clean timing repeat](https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington/actions/runs/33828854325)

The perf box’s normal queue and trust policy have been restored.
what should we do now?

We should turn the prototype into a real mbx feature, but avoid promoting performance claims yet. We’re tied with rust-cache, not convincingly ahead.

Recommended next steps:

1. Add a Cargo workspace-state sidecar to `mbx cache export/import`.
   - Preserve fingerprints, dep-info, build-script state, modes, timestamps, and CAS references.
   - Export the reachable CAS closure—not the entire raw store.

2. Implement hydration natively in Rust.
   - The Python hydrator currently costs about 2 seconds.
   - Parallel reflinking/materialization should bring that below roughly 500 ms, enough to move us from tied to a likely win.

3. Integrate it into `mr-boxington-action`.
   - Restore CAS closure, sidecar, and registry as one cache operation.
   - Keep the old cache format readable.

4. Run at least 7 paired GHA trials.
   - Reject cache misses and network errors automatically.
   - Report median, spread, archive size, restore, hydrate, and build separately.
   - I’d require at least a repeatable 5% end-to-end win before promoting it.

5. Once that passes, fold the small-edit scenario into the permanent benchmark and record results by mbx version.

The most valuable thing to do now is step 1: implement the sidecar in the actual cache export/import path. The storage measurement says the design is viable; the remaining job is eliminating the prototype’s restore overhead.
ok do it, make a pr, address pr feedback and failing checks until it settles

I’ll implement the production sidecar on a fresh branch from current `main`, integrate it with cache export/import and the action-facing workflow, add compatibility and restore tests, then open a ready-for-review PR. After that I’ll monitor review comments and CI, fixing issues until the PR is green and no actionable feedback remains.

const body = `## Summary

- add versioned named attachments to cache-export bundles while preserving v1 output for exports without attachments
- capture Cargo scheduler state at export without duplicating action outputs already present in CAS
- restore matching workspace state into an empty target using parallel reflink/copy materialization and an atomic rename
- preserve file modes and mtimes, recreate safe relative symlinks, and leave non-empty targets untouched
- document the automatic GitHub Action behavior

## Why

An mbx action-result closure can restore compiler outputs, but Cargo still needs its target scheduler metadata to recognize those outputs as fresh after a cache restore. Carrying that metadata alongside the closure makes the real-world small-edit case behave like a warm checkout. CAS-backed artifacts are referenced instead of packed a second time.

The prototype benchmark archive was 408.33 MiB versus rust-cache's 462.93 MiB (11.8% smaller), with only 55.78 MiB of inline scheduler state and manifest data added to the existing mbx bundle. In four paired small-edit trials the median end-to-end times were effectively tied: 38.904s for the hydrated mbx prototype and 38.980s for rust-cache. This PR turns that prototype into the native export/import path.

## Compatibility and safety

- exports with no attachments retain manifest version 1
- imports accept both v1 and v2 manifests
- attachment names and CAS roots are validated before import
- restore only targets an empty directory and stages all data before atomic placement
- equivalent checkouts can match by Cargo.toml/Cargo.lock signature when the absolute path differs

## Verification

- \`cargo clippy -p mbx -p mbx-cache-store --all-targets -- -D warnings\`
- \`cargo test -p mbx-cache-store --lib\`
- \`cargo test -p mbx -p mbx-cache-store\`
- end-to-end export/import test verifies Cargo treats restored output as fresh
- end-to-end safety coverage verifies non-empty targets are preserved and equivalent checkout paths restore correctly

Benchmark runs:
- composition: https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington/actions/runs/33827619024
- clean paired repeat: https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington/actions/runs/33828854325
`;

So v1.8 improved this scenario by roughly **34%**, but still trails rust-cache by **40%** even with registry caching.

The next performance PR should target two measured costs:

- Import/materialization: approximately **6.7s** slower than rust-cache. The current import writes, verifies, copies into CAS, then materializes 2.3 GiB into the target. We should adopt already-verified staged objects directly and preserve hardlink topology.
- Edited build: **15.44s vs 12.44s**. mbx synchronously publishes the changed 178 MiB executable; that work should move off the build-result critical path or use a zero-copy path where safe.

I left the benchmark work on `codex/gha-small-edit-benchmark` and did not open a promotional PR, because the honest result does not support the claim yet.
ok and we should do what we can to either test locally or test without needing to cut releases

Agreed. I’ll make the hosted harness accept an arbitrary mr-boxington ref: it will build mbx once, distribute that exact binary to every seed/measurement job, and keep the build itself outside the timed region. That lets us test a PR commit on real GitHub runners before releasing it; locally, we can use the same parent/export/fresh-import/child sequence to iterate on import phases quickly.

I’m turning the benchmark into a pre-release test loop now: arbitrary mbx refs, one untimed build shared across jobs, and configurable trial counts so a one-trial smoke test doesn’t burn a full matrix.

const patch = "*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: /tmp/mbx-small-edit.nZ4frt/.github/workflows/bench-refresh.yml
@@

     name: Measure ${{ matrix.tool }} (${{ matrix.trial }})
     needs: small-edit-seed
-    if: github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.small_edit
+    # `small-edit-seed` deliberately tolerates the candidate-build job being

+    if: always() && github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.small_edit && needs.small-edit-seed.result == 'success'
*** End Patch";

content.text:
No—mbx 1.8.0 is still slower than rust-cache in the real GitHub Actions small-edit test.

| Tool | Median build | Median restore + build |
|---|---:|---:|
| rust-cache | **12.8s** | **21.7s** |
| mbx-registry | 16.1s | 37.4s |
| mbx native bundle | 17.3s | 42.4s |

So our best mbx configuration is:

- **15.6s slower end-to-end**
- **72% slower than rust-cache**
- Trial range: 34.1–47.6s, versus rust-cache’s 19.3–25.8s

The main deficit is restore/setup overhead: about **21.3s for mbx-registry versus 9.0s for rust-cache**. The edited build itself is also approximately 3.3s slower.

[Run 33903592486](https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington/actions/runs/33903592486) contains the four trials. It also uncovered and verified a workflow skip bug; [PR #348](https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington/pull/348) fixes that, with all checks green and no review feedback.

Bottom line: we improved mbx substantially, but **we have not beaten rust-cache yet**. The next target is eliminating roughly 16 seconds from the mbx registry restore path.
